blockers.message: the review record has no `## code.review` section, while roles were active at it
R-skeptic-1 (The merge rests on "one e-mail = one person", which the design's own context contradicts) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it
R-skeptic-2 (Records are deleted with no way back) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it

findings.evidence:
Since an e-mail address identifies exactly one person, the job groups
customers by lower-cased e-mail, keeps the oldest record of each group,
moves the others' orders to it and deletes the others.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: The Context of the same design states the opposite: "Business customers often share a purchasing mailbox (`orders@acme.example`) between several buyers, each with their own customer record and billing address." Run as written, the job folds every buyer of such a company into the oldest one: their orders move to another person's record and their own name and billing address are deleted. Drop or qualify the assumption — e.g. merge only records whose e-mail AND name/billing address match, or exclude shared mailboxes — and add a spec scenario for "same e-mail, different buyers" stating that they are NOT merged.
findings.title: The merge rests on "one e-mail = one person", which the design's own context contradicts

findings.evidence: moves the others' orders to it and deletes the others.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: Deleting the duplicates is irreversible, and the plan gives no rollback, backup, audit trail of which order belonged to which record, or staged rollout (e.g. a dry-run report first). A wrong merge — see R-skeptic-1 — cannot be undone. Keep a mapping (old id → kept id, with the deleted row's data) or soft-delete, and add a dry-run task before the first real run.
findings.title: Records are deleted with no way back

findings.evidence: A nightly job SHALL merge customer records that share an e-mail address into the oldest one, moving their orders to it.
findings.recommendation: The only scenarios are "Two records, one e-mail" and "No duplicate". Nothing says whether `Ada@Example.org` and `ada@example.org` "share an e-mail address" (the design lower-cases, the spec does not say), which record wins on equal `created_at`, or what happens to a guest checkout inserting a customer or an order for a record while the job is merging it. Add scenarios for case differences, ties and a concurrent checkout.
findings.title: The spec covers only the happy path

findings.recommendation: The plan adds a scheduled nightly job ("A nightly job merges customers that share an e-mail address.") and rewrites existing production data (`orders.customer_id`, deletions in `customers`), yet operations and migration are unticked with no reason, so neither expert reviews it. Tick them, or give the reason on each line.
findings.title: Domains the plan touches are left unticked without a reason

findings.evidence: Guest checkouts create a new customer each time; support sees five records for one person.
findings.recommendation: `app/checkout.py` `guest_checkout` inserts a new customer on every call. The plan leaves that untouched, so duplicates keep appearing and support still sees them until the next nightly run. Weigh reusing an existing record at checkout (with the same identity rule as R-skeptic-1), or state why the nightly job alone is preferred.
findings.title: The Why names the cause, but the plan only cleans up after it

findings.evidence: - [ ] 1.1 Nightly merge job, verified by tests "Two records, one e-mail" and "No duplicate"
findings.recommendation: The tests verify the merge logic, not that the job is scheduled; the Impact lists only `jobs/merge_customers.py (new)`. Add a task, with an observable done state, that wires the job to the scheduler.
findings.title: No task makes the job run nightly
